• Observations show that average winter temperatures across the contiguous 48 states have increased by about 3°F since 1896. Spring temperatures have increased by about 2°F, while summer and fall temperatures have increased by about 1.6° [Note: These numbers reflect a data update through 2023 that is pending publication on EPA’s website.]
  • Temperature changes over the observed period vary by state, with larger seasonal increases across the northern states and the Mountain West, and smaller increases in the South and Southeast. All 48 states experienced winter warming over this time period. Most states experienced warming in the spring, summer, and fall, but a few states had little to no overall change or cooled slightly (for example, Alabama) during those months.
  • Like annual average temperature, the average temperature for each season is projected to continue to increase under all four greenhouse gas emissions scenarios. By about 2070, temperatures could stabilize or even begin to decline under the low emissions scenario, where there are significant reductions in greenhouse gas and other air pollutant emissions. Temperatures will continue to increase under the other three scenarios, however. Higher emissions lead to higher temperatures.
  • While winter has warmed more than other seasons so far, overall the projections suggest that all seasons will warm by a similar amount in the decades ahead, though with some regional differences.
